A Light For Your Camp 


NORA BAILEY — 1910-1951 


NO MOURNING—BY REQUEST 

“Come not to mourn for me, with solemn tread, 

Clad in dull weeds of sad and sable hue . . . 

. But wearing robes of emerald and blue. 

And dance, as I your dances oft have led. 

And laugh, as I have often laughed with y 
And be most merry— after I am dead. 

^Winifred Holtby) 


My first impulse on _ reading N 
Bailey’s article, “A Light for you 
Camp” was to do as I had so often 
donebefore, write to tell |«rl-^ 
I had liked it. It was a shock to reali 
-,,-u a letter could never now be writ 
ten, for Nora, having for many years 
endured what she rarely discussed, b 
"ce called an 'W' heart d ted » 
March, a few weeks before her article 
was published. 


Last Christmas’Nora told us some 

of the ideas she was thinking 
her essay 'We “yarned” about people 
camp’ camp. I remember 

she described the Chief at Ahmek a 
going around with the newest book 
on psychology in one hand, leaving 
other free to plant water likes or make 
Man drum^as the particular cummer 
rrvmired him. We mentioned a camp 

director who disturbed the best camp 

schedule by suddenly deciding 
should be a special day or a test 


occasion Nora remarked, with her 
typical humour, “Well, if as they say, 
camp’s supposed to be a democracy 
even the director should be^ free

the real light of the camp. ^ . t

to be- they know enough to be them 
?elve c !” These thoughts were expressed

anyone I know. 


Toronto, Canada, June, 1951 


7 




For many years Nora had been a 
camper, counselor, and personnel 
director at Gamp Wapomeo, which she 
loved. Here her joys of camper days 
blended with her professional psycho¬ 
logical skill to create a realistic and 
warm understanding of human living. 
She was always skeptical of what she 
called the “jabberwocky of her trade” 
and never allowed her psychology to 
obscure her humanity. Her own deep 
sensitivity was reflected in her genuine 
acceptance of people, and hundreds 
of Canoe Lake campers will recall the 
confidence she inspired and the gaiety 
she created. 

Nora attended Havergal College, and 
later took her arts degree at die Uni¬ 
versity of Toronto. This was followed 
by professional training at the Institute 
of Ghild Study where, in 1938, she 
wrote the first M.A, in psychology 
based on research in camping, thus 
setting a precedent for studies in this 
area. In T939, rather than being d’s-* 
mayed by her precarious hpart condi¬ 
tion, Nora signed on as sailmaker and 
spent eighteen months sailing around 
the world in the schooner Yankee . Her 
particulars duties were to look after 
the two young children of the skipper 
and his wife, but her other activities 
included standing . watch, scrubbing 
decks, and retaining morale through 
long days on turbulent seas. The letters 
from the voyage were mimeographed 
for circulation amongst her friends and 
through them she shared generously 
her vivid and exciting adventures. 

In 1948 Nora jo : ned the staff of the 
Mental Hygiene Institute in Montreal. 
Here, dealing with the problems of 
human living, she found expression for 
all her skills. Her deep distress at being 


unable to do all she saw should be done 
was expressed recently in a letter, the 
significance of which one realized only 
later: “Excuse me being hackneyed, 
but when I see all these people I can’t 
help remembering Cecil Rhodes — so 
much to do, so little time to do it.” 
It hurt Nora to be unable to meet any 
human need. 

All these had been good things in 
Nora’s life, but it was only in 1949 she 
achieved her real goal. This was Gamp 
Macuza, which she and Ruby Smith 
opened in the Laurentians for young 
boys and girls. We visited them that 
summer and found it a beautiful place. 
As we sat on the point in the evening, 
I asked Nora about the programme. 
She said, “Do you know what these 
children like doing best of all? They 
like playing hide-and-seek. There’s so 
little time in a modern child’s life to 
play hide-and-seek that we’ve decided 
our programme must have time and 
opportunity for campers* to do what 
they really' like to do. One is a ch : ld 
nowadays for such* a little while. Let 
the children have time to be them¬ 
selves.” 

It’s good to know that there’s such 
a place as Camp Macuza, where there 
is time for campers to do the important 
childish things of childhood. It is good 
to know that it is to continue, for Nora 
would have it so. And it’s good to know 
that there was a Light in the Gamp 
that spread its radiance throughout 
Canadian Camping. The light Nora 
Bailey kindled will gleam through all 
our campsites, and our darkness will 
be lightened by the privilege we have 
had in knowing a great “soul”. 

Mary L. N-orthway.

Canadian Camping 



TO A GROUP OF 

Counselors in Trmining 

By a Gamp Director 


You are a chosen group of old 
campers, who have experienced for 
several summers all the carefree hap¬ 
piness of those, whose chief concern at 
camp, is to have a good time. Your 
days as campers are now over, and you 
are returning in a different role. You 
are to be leaders—not, perhaps, with 
all the responsibility of full-fledged 
counselors, but certainly as counselors- 
in-training, or “counselors-to-be”. 

Because you have been campers and 
have a wealth of happy memories and 
many camp skills, and because you 
appreciate the high traditions and the 
aspects of good camping, I feel sure 
of your loyalty and your eagerness to 
share what you have gained with a 
younger group. Because camping is so 
essentially a real part of you, the oppor¬ 
tunity to pass on to others some of 
the joys that have been yours, will give 
you great satisfaction and scope for 
all the gifts you possess. 

The word “counselor” is a pleasant, 
happy word. At the first camp I 
attended, the leaders were called 
“officers”. That word suggests disci¬ 
pline (and no nonsense!), with a mili¬ 
tary flavor, and a rather impersonal 
relationship. But the modern word, 
“counselor”, suggests the friendly rela¬ 
tionship of comrade as well as leader. 

Perhaps, as you think back over your 
camp days, you can remember certain 
counselors whom you liked and respect¬ 
ed greatly. You probably admired 
them, not only for their skill and ability 
to do a good job in their particular 
field, whether it was crafts or swim¬ 
ming, music or sailing, but you admired 


them even more just for themselves— 
for their friendliness, their dependa¬ 
bility, their genuine interest in you. 
There were times, of course, when you 
tried to put something over on them, 
but you respected them all the more 
if they weren’t “easy”, if they didn’t 
play for popularity or shirk a duty be¬ 
cause it was difficult. You knew that 
the camp director expected high stan¬ 
dards from counselors in matters of 
discipline, punctuality and cheerful, 
willing teamwork, and you were bright 
enough to know and appreciate when 
a counselor measured up to these high 
standards. 

Now it is your turn to enter this 
role at camp—to pass on to a new and 
younger group all that has meant most 
to you. You probably realize that at 
this very moment there are swarms 
of children thinking and dreaming 
about their first days at camp. Their 
applications are in. They have read 
and re-read the folder and studied the 
pictures. They have begun to collect 
their outfit and perhaps to pack.their 
belongings. Some of them may have 
mixed feelings about going to camp. 
They have heard from school friends 
and parents about the fun they are 
goin£ to have, but they sometimes 
wonder, too, if they will be a bit lonely 
at times, for it will all be so new and 
strange. 

From the very first day, when you 
travel up with them on the train, right 
through the camp days,, as you follow 
the forest trails, explore the water-ways 
and get acquainted with them in their

So You Think Your Covered 

By M. H. Crone 
Maryland Casualty Company 

Canadian Managers—Robert Hampson & Son Limited—Montreal and Toronto 


In the last two issues we have dis¬ 
cussed the question of soft spots in your 
insurance programme, referring parti¬ 
cularly to your Fire and Liability Insur¬ 
ance as it applies to your business as a 
Camp operator. In this issue we thought 
it advisable to make some reference to 
your personal lines of coverage. 

To properly insure your house and 
its contents there are two forms of 
insurance recognized as providing the 
best coverage. 

On the building you should have a 
standard fire insurance policy to which 
is attached the Supplemental Perils 
Endorsement covering you against loss 
from Windstorm; Smoke Damage; from 
the unusual or faulty operation of your 
furnace; Aircraft or Vehicle Damage; 
Lightning Damage to electrical appli¬ 
ances; Riot; Civil Commotion and 
damage by water which is subject to 
a deductible of $15.00 from each claim. 
This policy also should provide for 
10% of the amount of insurance apply¬ 
ing to any outbuildings, such as your 
Garage, and up to 10% for the rent 
of any temporary abode should vou 
find it necessarv to live elsewhere fol¬ 
lowing a fire. If vou will examine your 
insurance in the light of these remarks 
the large majority of you will find that 
you are very much under-insured. 

Your household contents ' and per¬ 
sonal effects are not completely insured 
unless you are covered under what is 
known as a Personal Property Floater. 


It is of extreme importance to you fhat 
any valuable items such as Furs, Jewel¬ 
lery and Fine Arts be specifically sche¬ 
duled on this Policy. If you are in the 
habit of going off this Continent for 
vacation or business trips your policy 
should be endorsed to provide World 
Wide coverage. This policy in itself 
should be a subject for one publication 
and as we haven’t sufficient space, 
suffice it to say “See your agent” and 
make sure you are covered for an ade¬ 
quate sum and, most important of all, 
see that the form of cover is broad 
enough to protect you in all situations. 

That automobile you drive could put 
you into complete bankruptcy if not 
properly insured. The standard . limit 
of coverage for Public ..L'ability and 
Pronertv Damage is $5,000.00 for 
bodily iniury or death to one person, 
$10,000.00 for two or more persons in 
one accident, and $1,000.00 for Pro¬ 
perty Damage. These limits are as out¬ 
moded as Noah’s Ark. Court judg¬ 
ments for personal iniury have exceeded 
$100,000,00. Consider the amount of 
property damage you might be liable 
for it you were responsible for an acci¬ 
dent involving ,a loaded transport truck 
which burns as a result. The possible 
loss staggers the imagination and just 
imagine this; you can purchase an 
inclusive insurance limit of $100,000.00 
for only an additional cost of 24% on 
the portion of your premium which 
applies to these piimmum or standard 
limits. Don’t procrastinate on this one, 
change it to-day! 


10 


v Canadian Camping 



We presume you carry Collision, Fire 
and Theft on your car so won’t use up 
further space on these portions. If you 
have a radio it is not insured unless 
added to the Policy by endorsement. 
Flood, Windstorm, etc., should be 
added by attaching the Miscellaneous 
Cover endorsement at a cost of $1.00 
or $1.50 per year. Your insurance 
should be extended to protect you 
against third party claims should you 
be driving other automobiles, or from 
claims or damages from passengers in 
your own car. You may also have 
voluntary medical payments coverage 
on all passengers, including yourself, 
should you be injured in an automobile 
accident. Let me close this paragraph 
by simply stating that the bare auto¬ 
mobile policy does not provide you with 
proper coverage and a close examina¬ 
tion of your present coverage should be 
made without delay. 

Personage Liability Insurance is also 
an important coverage for you to con¬ 
sider. People can get hurt or property 
may be extensively damaged through 


your personal acts or those of your 
family. Common sources of these acci¬ 
dents are your family pets, golf, fishing, 
or other sports, unsafe sidewalks, steps, 
etc. This insurance may be purchased 
for as low as $7.50 for three years and 
should be a “must” on your program. 

In the large majority of businesses, 
employees are insured for personal acci¬ 
dents under our Compensation Laws, 
but what happens when the “Boss 
Man” is injured? You can protect 
your own income and insure your per¬ 
sonal out-of-pocket expenses by the 
purchase of Personal Accident Insur¬ 
ance. 

We have tried in these three articles 
to discuss your Insurance Problems in 
the language of a layman and hope that 
we have been successful in helping some 
of you to better understand the many 
complex problems which arise in choos¬ 
ing proper insurance coverage in return 
for the premium dollars which you are 
spending. 


What is Camping? 

Camping is not just an outing in the 
fresh air—it is an adventure in crea¬ 
tive living. 

Camping is not just learning the skills 
of the out-of-doors — it is learning 
how to work and play with others. 

Camping is more than fun and lots of 
it—it is the recreation and the re¬ 
making of body, mind and soul. 

Camping is more than living in “splen¬ 
did” isolation—it is the discovery of 
self through taking one’s rightful 
place in the life of a community. 

C. F. Plewman, 

Kilcoo Camp. 



Toronto , Canada , June, 1951

A Hanger’s Prayer . 

1 God help the folks who walk these trails 
Be mindful as they go 
That there shall be no embers left 
To tempt the winds that blow; 

Nor let them leave old tins about 
Their camp, or bits of glass 
For forest fires start from these 
Half-hidden in the grass. 

' This stream that runs its pebbled way, 

God, let them leave it sweet 
And pure as when they found it first 
‘ ' Hidden from summer’s heat. 

And do not let them cut the trees 
Thkt stand in majesty, 

Nor let them trample ferns, nor break 
The branches of the trees. 

‘"God keep my vision true and clear 
' Through all this blueish haze 
That hangs like velvet everywhere 
All these long summer days. 

Nor let me see a wisp of smoke 
Curl up where forests dwell, 

But if I do—God, give me strength 
.To do my duty well. 

G. Hastings. 


Conservation Pledge 


Prime Minister St. Laurent signed 
the Canadian Conservation pledge 
which appears below, and Canadian 
campers should be familiar with it, 
and challenged to accept it as a per¬ 
sonal pledge. 



I GIVE MY 

PLEDGE AS A CANADIAN 
TO SAVE AND FAITHFULLY TO 
DEFEND FROM WASTE THE 
NATURAL RESOURCES Of 
MY COUNTRY - ITS SOIL 
AND MINERALS, ITS 
FORESTS, WATERS 
AND WILDLIFE 




Toronto , Canada , June , 1951

Canadian Camping Association 
Report 

By Agnes Mutchler Executive Secretary 


In accordance with the instructions 
set out. in various minutes, a National 
Office was established last October. It 
was located in Montreal, in the vicinity 
of the President. In February of last 
year letters were sent to both the 
Quebec and the Ontario Associations 
in regard to sharing the costs of a 
National Office. Quebec f$lt no imme¬ 
diate need for quarters but offered to 
pay for services rendered. Ontario sent 
in an estimate on costs of setting up a 
joint office. 

After careful thinking it was decided 
that the National Office should be 
launched as a separate venture for two 
reasons: 

a The techniques, functions and 
routines of the GCA were not yet 
sufficiently defined to make possible 
an accurate estimate of the time 
that would be involved in the 
national work; 

b The state of the finances made it 
necessary to do things even more 
economically than the Ontario 
Executive considered a minimum. 

As you all realize, the office is experi¬ 
mental. Many things have been left 
undone. The GCA suffers from all the 
ills inherent in any volunteer organiza¬ 
tion. Sickness, births, deaths and the 
pressure of one’s own pre-occupation 
with earning a living—all impinge on 
the work of the organization. For in¬ 
stance, in October there were many 
sincere offers of volunteer secretarial 
work (my own office has been running 
not too awkwardlv on that basis for the 
past two years) volunteer mimeograph¬ 



ing and just simply—time. However, 
it was found that the heavy work 
periods of this office corresponded only 
too often with the times when volunteer 
offices were completely bogged down 
with their own affairs. The result was 
that your Executive Secretary has been 
involved in doing technical work quite 
beyond her skills and has simply tried 
to keep in touch with the membership. 
Letters have been answered and a flood 
of such material as the Constitution, 
Terms of Reference, etc., have gone 
out steadily. Now that we know that 
the pressure areas accumulate around 
the Board and Executive Meetings, to 
say nothing of the Annual Meeting, it 
should be possible to set dates and thus 
organize the volunteer help to better 
advantage. 

Some of the membership threads 
have been very tenuous and only after 
many letters had gone out would this 
office discover that the President had 
left the Province or the whole Executive 
had been swamped with other work. 
This meant an attempt to contact the 
individual membership. Finally letters 
began to come in and they opened 
almost consistently with one or the 
other of these statements, “Due to great 
personal pressures I have not been able 
. . . ” or, “In reply to your various 
letters ...” (all completely under¬ 
standable—but a little disconcerting). 

Each time mail goes out to the gen¬ 
eral membership more than 300 letters 
must be sent—for though all these are 
not members-in-good-standing — they 
are potential renewals. 


14 


Canadian Camping 



There are fifty Board Members listed, 
so that calling a Board Meeting in¬ 
volves at least twice that many letters, 
and in the case of a cancelled meeting, 
such as that planned for Queens in the 
Fall-—twice as many more. 

Material sent to Committee Chair¬ 
men has frequently brought no reply. 
Some have written of great discourage¬ 
ment but a determination to carry on, 
others have sent in tentative resigna¬ 
tions and still others have asked that 
the National Office set up their com¬ 
mittees. In connection with the latter, 
it was not until March of this year that 
we had even a nucleus of people who 
answered letters, let alone a list of 
potential committee members. 

Actually nothing could be more valu¬ 
able to the whole organization at this 
time than accurate camp directories 
compiled by each Province. Aside from 
requests by members for this kind of 
information, at least 20 letters have 
come from other organizations. The 
National Office would be grateful to 
have this kind of information to send 
out. 

When letters came in asking for 
definitions of committee function, I felt 
a little weak, for I knew of the hours 
that had been spent on just such defini¬ 
tions. Then I realized that when one 
works in the very heart of a well devel¬ 
oped camp area, enjoying a surfeit of 
the good things that come from com¬ 
panionship with knowledgable camp 
people, it is only too easy to forget that 
m areas of beginning and new camps, 
the needs are basic. That what seemed 
to the Executive i.ust fundamentals of 
good camping could seem to beginners 
as superstructure. It simply meant more 
letters, more questions, more hunting 
for other answers—more sensitivity to 
basic needs. 

The Camping Magazine does much 
to create a community of feeling among 
the distant camp members and it is 
one of the jobs of the National Office 
to supplement that good work with 


letters. It will be hard to create by mail 
that atmosphere which good-neighbor 
campers in Ontario and Quebec create 
from personal contacts. It can be done, 
but it will require constructive thinking 
on the part of all the more privileged 
CCA members. 

Not many areas have the advantage 
of attending the kind of conferences 
which have developed from years of 
experience in Quebec and Ontario. 
Copies of this material should go out 
at least to the Executives in other pro¬ 
vinces. The charming Camp brochures 
that hang on the bulletin board in the 
office are full of suggestions and pic¬ 
tures of camp life that are absolutely 
stimulating. They, too, might go out 
from the Central office. 

The National Office of the CCA is 
a struggling child. Bludgeoning the 
infant is hardly regarded as good tech¬ 
nique. The parent who rescued a newly 
planted lawn from the gardening opera¬ 
tions of his offspring and was able to 
find extenuating circumstances, because 
when he was young he had received 
great charity, seems to be the mature 
approach that is needed to help the 
whole CCA grow up. 

Each membership card issued in the 
CCA represents more than just another 
member. It represents a group of camp- 
minded people who have come to sit 
around a central camp fire. This fire 
will burn low at times, because it must 
be fuelled by energy, time, money and 
faith. From this fire must go the begin¬ 
ning light to kindle fires in each pro¬ 
vince. B.C. with its opportunity for real 
forest camps, Alberta whose foothills 
are wondrous ranch country, Manitoba 
with Lake Wmnipeg and pastoral coun¬ 
tryside, Saskatchewan with its almost 
hidden vallevs and lakes, the Maritimes 
with their lovely sea coves—each of 
these can bring brands to the central 
fire. Every Camper knows that tending 
the fire can be long and tedious. It 
would seem that this unspectacular job 
; s the bas ; c function of the National 
Office. One day this fire will blaze! 


'Toronto, Canada, ]une, 1951

sizes and quantities you

Toronto, Canada, June> 1953 



NOTES 

from the Provinces 

BRITISH COLUMBIA 

The Annual Meeting of the British 
Columbia Camping Association on 
April 27th brought to a close an inter¬ 
esting year for the association. Miss 
Phyllis Porter, the president for the 
past year, took office as a newcomer in 
the group. She is to be congratulated 
on the success of the year’s program. 
Miss Porter is on the staff of Alexandra 
Neighborhood House and has had a 
wide experience in camping. Last 
summer she was a counselor in a camp 
in Hawaii. 

The program of the Annual Meeting 
included the usual election of officers 
and reports of activities during the 
year. The highlight being the report 
of the handcraft course sponsored by 
the association. There were 38 regis¬ 
trations, representing 10 association 
members camps and several other 
camps not members. Instruction in 
crafts chosen by the group was given, 
with special emphasis on crafts suitable 
to camps. It is hoped that the interest 
created this year in this course will 
enable us to introduce a course next 
season in campcraft. Following the 
reports, there were skits, based on inci¬ 
dents in the association during the 
eleven years since its organization. 
These may have been serious problems 
at the time, but looking hack, seemed 
very humorous. 

The guest speaker of the evening 
was Bishop A. H. Sovereign, recently 
retired Bishop of Athabasca, and a 
pioneer in camping for children in 
British Columbia. His stories of the 
early days and his words of wisdom for 
us were a genuine inspiration. 


ONTARIO 

It was with great regret that the 
Ontario Camping Association learned 
of the resignation of Mr. C. T. Sharpe, 
who has served for the past three years 
as superintendent of camping under the 
Department of Education of the On¬ 
tario Government. During these years 
Mr. Sharpe has made a unique contri¬ 
bution to the whole camping movement 
in this province. He possesses a wide 
knowledge of camping, gained during 
his long experience as a camp leader; 
he has a sympathetic understanding of 
the many problems facing the institu¬ 
tional camps operating on the prover¬ 
bial “shoe string”, and he has helped 
greatly in working out Camp Standards 
and in promoting more and better 
facilities for an ever-increasing number 
of children. All these things combined 
to make C. T. Sharpe specially fitted 
for his job. He served his government 
with distinction. It is to be hoped that 
the good work of the government will 
“carry on” with regard to camp subsi¬ 
dies, counselor training courses and the 
government training camps for boys 
and girls.

Canadian Camping 



MHWK REVIEWS 

GOING TO CAMP (a Guide to Good 

Camping) by Helen Beck; Ryerson 

Press, Toronto, 1950; pp. 164; illus¬ 
trations by Max Barris. 

There are many camping books for 
adults; this is for children. In direct, 
descriptive language, it informs the 
child how to prepare for and what to 
expect at that place, Camp . It gives 
to twelve-year-olds practical informa¬ 
tion on how to get ready—what the 
journey and first days of camp are like 
— what may happen during camp 
through the summer and some of the 
characteristics of coming home. It in¬ 
cludes a list of camp equipment and a 
glossary of camp “lingo”. Perhaps one 
might call it a child’s guide to adults, 
for it suggests what the camper should 
do both about the counselor (glossary 
definition, “person in charge of a group 
of children”) and about his parents— 
how to write to them, how to entertain 
them when they visit and how to help 
them adapt to the new self that arrives 
•home. 

I like the matter-of-fact tone and the 
frankness with which the authors state 
that although camp provides many 
exciting things such as interesting ani¬ 
mals and counselor hunts, it also has its 
own requirements such as being quiet in 
rest hour and putting your very own 
money in the camp office. I imagine 
that children, too, would like the book, 
though I am not certain that they’ll 
remember to send sister a birthday card 
just because they’ve read this sugges¬ 
tion in printed form. However, it will 
help them prepare and to understand 
and, at most, it will enable them to 
say, “but we didn’t do things that way 
at our camp”. It is realistic rather than 
sentimental, and children will certainly 
appreciate that. M.L.N. 

GAMP SITES AND FACILITIES by 

Bov Scouts of America, 2 Park Ave., 

New York 16, N.Y. $2.50. 


This well-illustrated and carefully 
prepared manual is intended to help 
local Boy Scout authorities design and 
develop their camp sites. In this type 
of camping, various scout troops use 
a district camp, in some cases preparing 
their own food, usually running their 
own program, but making use of the 
central facilities for water supply, sani¬ 
tation, medical care and some other 
items. However, the material supplied 
in this book can be adapted readily to 
most Canadian camp settings. The sec¬ 
tions on sanitation, water supply and 
kitchen layout are especially useful. 
The book contains a wealth of detailed 
information on many aspects of camp 
layout, which would be useful to camp 
directors, and to organisations owning 
camps. Technical details of interest to 
engineers and architects are included. 

Chapters are devoted to the Master 
Plan, Property, Site Development Plan, 
Water Supply, Sewage and Garbage 
Disposal, Program Facilities, Aquatic 
Facilities, Roads and Trails, Buildings, 
Land Management and Bibliography. 

R.K.C. 


MORE FUN IN THE WATER by* 
Eidola J. Bourgaize, published by 
Association Press, N.Y., 1950; pp. 
118; price $2,50. Available in Canada 
from the G. R. Welch Co., 1149 King 
St. W., Toronto. 

The title of this book is self-explana¬ 
tory. It is a veritable encyclopedia of 
games, stunts, water parties, water 
pageants for the landlubber, novice, 
average swimmer and the “old salt”. 
Instructions are clearly and simply ex¬ 
pressed and equipment, if needed, is 
kept at a minimum and is easily obtain¬ 
able. This excellent book would make 
program planning for a watersport’s 
day simple. There are also countless 
suggestions for “free play” swim 
periods. A useful book for waterfront 
directors or counselors.

THE GAMP PROGRAM BOOK,, by 
Catherine T. Hammett and Virginia 
Musselman, in collaboration with the 
National Recreation Association; 

published May, 1951, by the Associa¬ 
tion Press, N.Y.; available in Canada 
from the G. R. Welch Co., 1149 King 
St. W., Toronto; pp. 500; price $6.25. 

Emphasizing camp program as a 
whole , the encyclopedic handbook de¬ 
scribes in detail what happens/and how 
it happens. It shows how camp activi¬ 
ties can develop out of natural situations 
and how good leadership can make a 
camp program that is much more than 
separate activities in which campers are 
expected to take part. 

Based oil a philosophy that camping 
is living and * learning together in the 
out-of-doors, and doing things that 
can’t be done in town, this book organ¬ 
izes all the specialist information and 
know-how on 

Program Planning—what it is, the 
influence of the site, types of 
groups, mechanics. 

Living in the Out-of-Doors—“camp¬ 
keeping”, campcraft skills, fires, 
cooking, nature, hikes, waterfront, 
construction projects. 

Related Program Activities—arts and 
crafts, sports, cabin-door games, 
music, dramatics, ' story-telling, 
creative writing, photography, 
health and safety, discussions, indi¬ 
vidual activities, infirmary activi¬ 
ties. 

Composite Activities — evening pro¬ 
grams, campfires, festivals and holi¬ 
days, clubs and hobbies, traditions, 
intercultural, spiritual welfare, the 
Sabbath, visitors’ day, opening and 
closing camp, play ceremonies, 
international programs. 


Specific Plans for Programs—intro¬ 
ducing the staff, closing day ban¬ 
quet, an indoor beach party, the 
order of the torch, a tribal meet, 
a camp war game, how a fishing 
program got started, an Olympic 
beach party, an African Safari, a 
Fourth’ of July program, a camp 
country fair, a sleeping beauty 
pageant. 

The Camp Program Book is a one- 
volume encyclopedia on everything that 
goes into camp life as it relates to the 
camper. Everything in one BIG book!

Following are some hints to camp leaders which will help to win and sustain 
the confidence and respect of campers, and will tend to minimize misconduct. 

1. Know as many campers as possible by name. In addition, know something 
about them. 

2. Be friendly. Always show interest in what individual campers are doing and 
what progress they are making in school, hobbies or other activities in whic 
they are participating. 

3. Commend good qualities and actions. 

4. Try to be constructive, not repressive, in all dealings with them. 

5. Remember that a sense of humor is extremely valuable. 

6. When necessary, be firm. At all times, be fair! 

7. Do not judge misconduct solely on how much it annoys you. 

8. Do not take your personal feelings and prejudices out on them. 

9. Be consistent in all your dealings. 

10. Maintain poise at all times. Do not lose your temper. 

11. Remember—“The tongue is the only keen-edged tool which grows sharper 
with constant use”. Do not nag, bluff, or be officious. 

12. Try to see their side of the question. 

13. Look for the good qualities—everyone of them have them. 

14. Do not “pick” on every “little thing” they do. Sometimes it is wiser to 
overlook some things. 

15. Bear in mind that misbehaviour is seldom wilful. There usually is a cause, 
and it may be in yourself, the activity, or some other outside influence. 

16. Check program and facilities constantly. Study attendance and listen to 
their suggestions and complaints. 

17. Repair damages immediately. Remove markings from walls as soon as 
possible. Have* broken windows repaired without delay. 

18. Follow up all cases which have been disciplined. Be certain that you still 
have the respect and confidence of the camper. 

19. Be sincere in your work. 

20. Set a .good example yourself. 

—Adapted from Youth Leaders Digest .

To obtain best results in transplant¬ 
ing trees, great care should be taken 
in lifting .and replanting. The roots 
should be injured as little as possible. 
This will mean digging a trench around 
each tree at a radius of one and one- 
half feet or more from the trunk to a 
depth of about one and. a half feet. 

After the trenching is finished, strong 
burlap of sufficient size to envelop 
completely the ball of soil around the 
roots, may be laid into the trench at 
one side. The tree and ball of soil 
should then be gently eased onto the 
burlap; at the same time unsevered 
anchor roots should be cut with a sharp 
spade. Fold and tie the burlap securely 
around the ball of soil in readiness for 
transporting the tree to its new locatiop. 

When moving trees from the woods, 
those growing in high land or in soil 
similar to that into which they are to

be transplanted, should be selected. It 
may also be advisable to prune back 
some of the outermost branches of 
broadleaf trees. A small tree with a 
good fibrous root system will grow 
faster and be more healthy than a 
larger tree moved with few feeding 
roots.

NATURE ALPHABET 

Cap’n Bill Vinal, who was one of 
the outstanding leaders at the Quebec 
Camp Conference, has written a great 
deal on nature lore. A useful pamphlet 
called “Nature Games’ 3 , can be pur¬ 
chased for the paltry sum of fifteen 
cents, by writing William G. Vinal, 
Nature Education, University of Massa¬ 
chusetts, Amherst, Mass. From this 32 
page booklet of valuable material, we 
quote one game—Nature Alphabet. 

The leader names a letter of the 
alphabet. Each player in order names 
a bird, flower or tree (decided upon 
before starting) which begins with that 
letter. Anyone who cannot do so in 
less than five seconds is out. No one is 
to name an object which has already 
been named. The patrol having the 
greatest number at the end of a certain 
time is the winner or the last group 
to name an object commencing with 
that letter wins a point for his team. 


“BUDDY BURNER’ 3 

I am indebted to the Girl Scouts of 
America for this gadget which they 
call a “Buddy Burner”. Take a small 
tin about 2V2 inches high and 3 inches 
in diameter, such as a canned chicken 
or salmon tin or a “cut down” soup tin. 
Fill it almost full with melted wax, 
such as ends of candles or paraffin wax. 
Take a strip of corrugated cardboard 
about two feet Ion*? and the width of 
the height of the tin. Roll it up and 
place in the soft wax. This serves as 
a wick. This gives you a small fire 
that you can use under a No. 10 can 
stove, and I have been told that it wdl 
keep the stove hot about an hour. It 
is a very satisfactory blaze and can be 
used safely where it would be impos¬ 
sible to light a fire. The cover of the 
tin can, plaved over the flame, puts 
out your fire quickly and efficiently. 

M.G. 


BANDY BALL 

At the Quebec Camp Conference 
we were introduced to a new game with 
interesting possibilities. It is called 
“Bandy Ball”. It resembles an over¬ 
grown badminton bird with a rubber 
base about 2 1 /2 // i n diameter and a 
“cFown” of stiff, strong tail feathers. 
Instead of being batted with a racquet, 
it is returned by striking the round rub¬ 
ber end with the open palm. It is a 
game for which many variations can 
be improvised. Since neither courts, 
nets or racquets are necessary, one can 
think of exciting games being played 
by a team, across a tightened rope or 
players standing in marked circles. 

One game suggested is for players 
to stand inside opposite circles—about 
ten feet across. One player serves the 
bandy ball—the object being to bat 
it back and forth in the air with the 
open hand. The serve must be under¬ 
hand; the ball is “dead” when it touches 
the ground. The service changes after 
each five points are scored. The area 
inside the circle is fair territory; out¬ 
side is foul. Points are scored against 
player or side who (1) fail to return 
ball to opponent’s circle; (2) hits ball 
into a “foul”; (3) permits ball to touch 
ground inside his own circle. First 
player or side to score twenty-one points 
wins. 

Since we do not know of anyone else 
who has imported this new game, we 
give the name of the exhibitor at the 
Quebec Camp Conference, Joey Rich¬ 
mond, 399 St. Catherine Street West, 
Montreal. Price of Bandy Ball, $1.00. 

M.S.E. 

Whether a counselor is called an 
instructor or a leader is unimportant; 
what is important is that every coun¬ 
selor shall BE a leader, first, foremost 
and all the time. 

John Hoyle, Camp Gay Venture.

BUTTON! BUTTON! WHO'S GOT THE BUTTON? 


Why, Canadian Campers, of Course! 

By wearing the attractive new button, you announce: 

“I am one of a great company right across Canada 
who enjoy the grand adventure of camping.” 

But more than this: You are helping a most worthy cause. 

The Canadian Camping Association holds a charter from 
our government, authorizing it as the approved organization 
to sponsor and promote good camping standards throughout 
Canada. From east to west, we campers are linked together 
through membership in a great camping fraternity. Sale of 
these small emblems helps our National organization to 
finance its valuable work of promotion and publications. 



The button is sold to campers for a nominal fee (10c or 25c). 
Every button SOLD helps the Canadian Camping Association. 
Every button WORN shows you are a Canadian camper. 


DIRECTORS: Please detach this page and put it on your camp notice board. Promote the 
idea and plan some special celebration each month at camp, for which a button is the 
admission ticket. 

Order from C.C.A. office, 771 Burnside Avenue, Montreal, or after June-10th, from 
Miss Dais Gass, Camp Memphramagog, Mansonville, Quebec. 

Ontario campers—O.C.A. office, 52 Avenue Road, Toronto, or after June 20th, from 
Miss Joyce Bertram, Camp Ouareau, Montcalm County, Quebec. 

Make cheques payable to the Canadian Camping Association. 

(It is recommended that the button be sold in private camps for twenty-five cents and 
in institutional camps at ten cents).

A PRAYER FOR CAMP LEADERS 

Lord of Creation and Author of all 
things true and beautiful, we humbly 
lift our hearts in gratitude for the 
wonder of Thy world, and for eyes to 
see the pageantry of days and nights 
and changing seasons. We thank Thee 
for the adventure and responsibility of 
leadership among children in their holi¬ 
day time. Since Thou art the source 
of all wisdom , we seek to draw from 
Thy limitless resources/ lest we fail in 
our task . 

Take from us a false sense of our 
own sufficiency. Deepen our awareness 
of Thy all-prevailing Presence about us 
and within us, so that at all times we 
may have poise, confidence, understand¬ 
ing and a sense of humor. 

Grant that we may pass on to our 
campers the best Thou canst give to 
them through the medium of our rela¬ 
tionship. Make us instruments worthy 
of the opportunity which lies before us. 
May we see with them the wonder of 
each new day, feel their joyous zest for 
living, and grasp in our minds the 
amaz'ngfpotentiality of each young life. 

Help-us in our camps to build bridges 
of friendship and understanding be¬ 
tween our campers and between peoples 
of different races -and creeds, so that 
we, together, may play our part in 
building a better world for Th)> great 
family of mankind.

TTo Success In Ctemping! 


The secret lies in always keeping up to 
date with the latest ideas in 
organized camping. 

Success is built on ideas. Continued success 
depends on new ideas you obtain and use 
in the future. The best way to keep abreast 
of latest camping developments, say thou¬ 
sands of successful camping people, is by 
joining the American Camping Assn, and 
by regularly reading the up-to-the-minute, 
authoritative articles which appear each 
month in the magazine serving camps. 

Alert camp directors and their staffs read 
about tried and proved ideas in the latest 
CAMPING MAGAZINE and CAMPING 
MAGAZINE'S Annual Reference and Buying 
Guide issue. They know the danger of 
static thinking and obsolete ideas. You, too, 
will find these publications a never-ending 
source of new, usable ideas. 

Membership includes your subscription to 
these publications, and many more valuable 
benefits, costs $3.00 to $25.00 per year, 
depending on classification. For full infor¬

In Lighter Vein 

'Once there was a camper 

And how her trunk did cram 
With candy, nuts and biscuits, 
Olives, cheese and jam. 

Word passed around the section— 
“When the hour grows late, 

Steal away, without a light. 

This is a special date!” 

Within a crowded cabin 
They sat on bed and floor 
Emptying jars and boxes 
And bottles by the score. 

It really seems a pity 
This lovely tale to spoil, 

But they all submitted later 
To a dose of castor oil! 

M.S.E.

Our swimming counselor is going to 
give us half an hour of artificial 
inspiration!” 

The trouble with the modern child 
(The wild and wilful one) 

He’s ne’er been tanned by anything 
Except the summer sun!
